title: Memory management and virtual memory
subtitle: Programs think they own a huge private address space. The OS and the MMU make that true with pages, page tables, and a policy for what to throw out.

sections.title: Contiguous allocation and fragmentation
sections.body: The simplest scheme gives each process one contiguous block. The OS keeps a list of free holes and, for each request, chooses one: first fit takes the first hole big enough, best fit the smallest that fits, worst fit the largest. Whatever is left over is too small to use — external fragmentation. Compaction can squeeze holes together but costs a great deal of copying.

questions.prompt: Free holes are 100, 500, 200, 300, 600 KB. Which policy can place all four requests 212, 417, 112, 426?

choices.text: Best fit — the others strand memory and leave 426 unplaced.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: First fit and worst fit carve big holes into pieces that no longer fit 426; best fit keeps the large holes whole (result: 212→B4 417→B2 112→B3 426→B5).

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It leaves 1 request unplaced: 426 KB has no hole left once 212 and 112 have split the 500 KB block.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It also fails on 426 KB (1 unplaced) because it keeps shaving the largest hole.

sections.title: Paging
sections.body:
Paging cuts the virtual address space into fixed-size pages and physical memory into same-size frames. Any page can go in any frame, so external fragmentation disappears. A per-process page table maps page number → frame number; a virtual address splits into a page number and an offset, and the offset passes through unchanged.

With 4 KB pages, the address 0x3A7C has page number 3 and offset 0xA7C; if page 3 lives in frame 9, the physical address is 9·4096 + 0xA7C. A small cache of recent translations, the TLB, keeps this fast.

worked.why: 4 KB pages → 12 offset bits. Virtual address 0x3A7C: page number = 0x3A7C >> 12 = 3, offset = 0xA7C.
If page 3 is in frame 9, the physical address is frame × 4096 + offset = 36864 + 2684.

questions.prompt: During translation, what happens to the offset bits?

choices.text: They are multiplied by the frame number.
They pass through unchanged — only the page number is replaced by a frame number.
They are looked up in the page table.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Nothing is multiplied; the frame number is shifted into the high bits.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Pages and frames are the same size, so a byte keeps its position inside the page.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The page table is indexed by page number only.

sections.title: Page replacement
sections.body:
Virtual memory keeps only some pages resident. A reference to a non-resident page is a page fault: the OS loads it from disk and, if no frame is free, must evict another. FIFO evicts the oldest resident page; LRU the least recently used; LFU the least frequently used; the unreachable optimal policy evicts the page needed furthest in the future and serves as the yardstick.

On the textbook reference string with 3 frames: FIFO = 15 faults, LRU = 12, optimal = 9 of 20 references.

questions.prompt: Why does LRU usually beat FIFO?

choices.text: Programs show locality: a page used recently is likely to be used again soon, while an old page may still be hot.
LRU never faults more than FIFO.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The opposite: exact LRU needs bookkeeping on every reference.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: FIFO only knows age of loading; LRU tracks use, which is what predicts the future.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Not a theorem; it tends to win on real programs, not on every string.

sections.title: Belady's anomaly and thrashing
sections.body:
More frames should mean fewer faults — but not for FIFO. On the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, three frames give 9 faults and four frames give 10: Belady's anomaly. LRU and optimal are stack algorithms and cannot do this.

Thrashing is the other failure: if the frames given to a process are fewer than its working set, it faults almost every reference and the CPU idles while the disk churns. The fixes are to give it enough frames, or to suspend some processes.

questions.prompt: FIFO with 4 frames faults more than with 3 on the same string. What does this show?

choices.text: Four frames is too many for this string.
Adding memory does not always help FIFO — Belady's anomaly.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It is a real, classic result reproduced exactly by the textbook string.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: More frames can never be “too many”; the policy is at fault.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: FIFO's eviction order ignores use, so a larger memory can shift which pages are resident at the wrong moment (9 → 10 faults).

problems.prompt: Reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1 with 3 frames: count faults for FIFO, LRU and optimal.

sections.title: Segmentation and allocating frames
sections.body:
Segmentation divides a program by meaning — code, data, stack — rather than by fixed size. An address is (segment, offset); a segment table holds each segment's base and limit, and an offset beyond the limit is a protection fault. Segments are visible to the programmer and variable-sized, so they bring back external fragmentation; real systems combine both ideas (paged segments).

Given a segment table, translate (2, 100): if segment 2 has base 4300 and limit 400, then 100 < 400 is legal and the physical address is 4300 + 100 = 4400; offset 500 would trap.

worked.why: Check the offset against the limit.

questions.prompt: Segment 2 has base 4300 and limit 400. What happens for (2, 500)?

choices.text: A protection fault — the offset exceeds the limit.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Adding base and offset without checking the limit is the bug segmentation prevents.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: There is no wrap-around; out-of-range is an error.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The limit register exists precisely to stop a program reaching beyond its own segment.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Paging removes external fragmentation; the page table maps pages to frames, the offset is unchanged.
  • A page fault loads from disk; the replacement policy decides the victim.
  • Optimal ≤ LRU ≲ FIFO on real programs; FIFO can even get worse with more frames.
  • Thrashing = fewer frames than the working set.
